title.narrative: Child labour innovation models to boost impact

description.narrative: The first part of the project was about testing innovative approaches to collect data on child labor. Measuring child labor is a big challenge for the cocoa industry. To close this gap, qualitative and quantitative data collection including indirect questioning methods was carried out with cocoa farmers. In the qualitative data collection, 36 in-depth one-hour interviews were conducted by an anthropologue with farmers on their attitude towards child labor. Findings include that:• Farmers recognize the risks/cost associated with children working;• Farmers recognize the illegality of child labour;• Farmers report a lack of trust to report on child labour; and• Farmers are not willing to reveal child labour (see also below).In the quantitative data collection, data from 1,741 cocoa producers working with Barry Callebaut in Côte d’Ivoire were collected to estimate whether child labor prevalence could be elicited from parents using indirect elicitation methods such as the list experiment or the color box method. Findings include that parents underreport child labour when answering direct questions in face-to-face interviews. More importantly there is only a weak evidence for whether this bias can be overcome by the use of indirect elicitation methods such as list experiments and color box method. Evidence from the qualitative data collection suggests that the reason for this finding was due to cocoa farmers being well informed and very concerned about legal sanctions. Farmers also expressed low levels of trust towards most stakeholders involved in child labour prevention, including researchers. It was therefore concluded that direct and indirect questioning are not sufficient to overcome child labour estimates misreported by parents. In other words, measuring child labour is not feasible by questioning adults, irrespective of the data collection method.The second part of the CLIMB project comprised the collection of community and school infrastructure data of the entire cocoa sourcing region in Côte d’Ivoire collected by the non-profit organization Enveritas. This community data helps to understand the child labor risk factors as well as the access to services that help protect children in cocoa-growing communities. Enveritas visited 1,676 cocoa communities in Côte d’Ivoire between July and October 2021 and conducted a total of 21,966 surveys.Findings include:• Regarding community infrastructure, over 80% of households have access to electricity and drinking water and a phone network available. However, for other services accessibility is a key challenge (e.g. the average distance to the nearest paved road is 3.5 hours of walk.)• 99% of cocoa communities have access to at least one primary school generally less than 3 km away from the community center. Pre- and secondary schools are further away.• Most of the children in cocoa growing communities are enrolled in primary school. However, school infrastructure is precarious - around one third has water and usable-gender separated toiles, 13% have electricity, and only 4% have a canteen that runs more than half of the school year.This community data set and findings are available to any interested stakeholder. The data is used to better understand root causes and local context of child labour, inform the community approach strategy and prioritize communities to receive support.
